passages.text: The proportion of endometrial tumours associated with Lynch syndrome (PETALS): A prospective cross-sectional study

Lynch syndrome (LS) predisposes to endometrial cancer (EC), colorectal cancer, and other cancers through inherited pathogenic variants affecting mismatch-repair (MMR) genes. <sentence_start/>Diagnosing LS in women with EC can reduce subsequent cancer mortality through colonoscopic surveillance and aspirin chemoprevention; it also enables cascade testing of relatives. <sentence_start/>A growing consensus supports LS screening in EC; however, the expected proportion of test positives, and optimal testing strategy is uncertain. <sentence_start/>Previous studies from insurance-based healthcare systems were limited by narrow selection criteria, failure to apply reference standard tests consistently, and poor conversion to definitive testing. <sentence_start/>The aim of this study was to establish the prevalence of LS and the diagnostic accuracy of LS testing strategies in an unselected EC population.

This was a prospective cross-sectional study carried out at a large United Kingdom gynaecological cancer centre between October 2015 and January 2017. <sentence_start/>Women diagnosed with EC or atypical hyperplasia (AH) were offered LS testing. <sentence_start/>Tumours underwent MMR immunohistochemistry (IHC), microsatellite instability (MSI), and targeted <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-methylation testing. <sentence_start/>Women <50 years, with strong family histories and/or indicative tumour molecular features, underwent MMR germline sequencing. <sentence_start/>Somatic MMR sequencing was performed when indicative molecular features were unexplained by LS or <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-hypermethylation. <sentence_start/>The main outcome measures were the prevalence of LS in an unselected EC population and the diagnostic accuracy of clinical and tumour testing strategies for risk stratifying women with EC for MMR germline sequencing. <sentence_start/>In total, 500 women participated in the study; only 2 (<1%) declined. <sentence_start/>Germline sequencing was indicated and conducted for 136 and 135 women, respectively. <sentence_start/>A total of 16/500 women (3.2%, 95% CI 1.8% to 5.1%) had LS, and 11 more (2.2%) had MMR variants of uncertain significance. <sentence_start/>Restricting testing to age <50 years, indicative family history (revised Bethesda guidelines or Amsterdam II criteria) or endometrioid histology alone would have missed 9/16 (56%), 8/13 (62%) or 9/13 (69%), and 5/16 (31%) cases of LS, respectively. <sentence_start/>In total 132/500 tumours were MMR deficient by IHC of which 83/132 (63%) had <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-hypermethylation, and 16/49 (33%) of the remaining patients had LS (16/132 with MMR deficiency, 12%). <sentence_start/>MMR-IHC with targeted <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-methylation testing was more discriminatory for LS than MSI with targeted methylation testing, with 100% versus 56.3% (16/16 versus 9/16) sensitivity (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.016) and equal 97.5% (468/484) specificity; 64% MSI-H and 73% MMR deficient tumours unexplained by LS or <italic toggle="yes">MLH1-</italic>hypermethylation had somatic MMR mutations. <sentence_start/>The main limitation of the study was failure to conduct MMR germline sequencing for the whole study population, which means that the sensitivity and specificity of tumour triage strategies for LS detection may be overestimated, although the risk of LS in women with no clinical or tumour predictors is expected to be extremely low.

In this study, we observed that age, family history, and histology are imprecise clinical correlates of LS-EC. <sentence_start/>IHC outperformed MSI for tumour triage and reliably identified both germline and somatic MMR mutations. <sentence_start/>The 3.2% proportion of LS-EC is similar to colorectal cancer, supporting unselected screening of EC for LS.
Emma Crosbie and colleagues investigate the prevalence of and strategies for identifying Lynch syndrome among women with endometrial cancer.

Endometrial (womb) cancer (EC) is the most common gynaecological cancer in the developed world, and its incidence is rising. <sentence_start/>A significant minority (around 3%) of EC are caused by an inherited genetic predisposition called Lynch syndrome (LS).

EC may be the first sign that a woman has LS. <sentence_start/>She is likely to survive this cancer but develop other preventable cancers related to LS later in life. <sentence_start/>Her family members are also at risk.
Identifying women with LS can enable them to reduce their risk of new cancers, for example, through bowel (colorectal) cancer surveillance (colonoscopy).
We do not know how many women with EC have LS or how best to identify them; current practice is based on experience in bowel cancer and may not be accurate in EC.
What did this research do and find?
We tested 500 women with EC treated in a large tertiary referral centre in the North West of England for LS.

We did not preselect women to test based on clinical or tumour characteristics. <sentence_start/>We tested tumours for features of LS called mismatch repair (MMR) deficiency and microsatellite instability (MSI). <sentence_start/>Women with strongly suggestive clinical or tumour characteristics underwent germline LS testing.
In total, 16 of 500 women (3%) had LS, and these women could not always be predicted by their age or family history.
MMR deficiency was more accurate than MSI at identifying LS-EC, picking up 16/16 (100%) versus 9/16 (56%).
In our study, we found that 3% of women with endometrial cancer have LS and can benefit from strategies to reduce their future cancer risk.
Our results suggest that it may be best to test everyone because preselecting women to test based on clinical or tumour characteristics misses cases of LS.
In this population, tumour MMR deficiency was more accurate than MSI at identifying LS in EC.
Our results should be interpreted with caution because we did not do germline testing on all women, and the number of women we tested was relatively small.

Endometrial cancer (EC) is the most common gynaecological cancer in developed countries, and incidence is rising [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref001" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/14651858" pmcid="PMC10845858" pmid="25549990" count="1">1</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Although mostly driven by obesity and decreased parity, a significant minority is caused by Lynch syndrome (LS), an inherited susceptibility to defective DNA mismatch repair (MMR). <sentence_start/>At least 1:280 of the general population carries a pathogenic variant in an MMR gene-<italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MSH2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MSH6</italic> or <italic toggle="yes">PMS2</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">path_MMR</italic>)<italic toggle="yes">-</italic>the vast majority of whom are undiagnosed [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref002" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1055-9965.EPI-16-0693" pmid="27799157" pmcid="PMC5336409" count="1">2</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The risks of EC, ovarian cancer (OC), and colorectal cancer (CRC) in <italic toggle="yes">path_MMR</italic> heterozygotes are approximately 35%, 11%, and 46%, respectively [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref003" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/gutjnl-2015-309675" pmid="26657901" pmcid="PMC5534760" count="1">3</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These risks are significantly higher than for the general population (EC-3%, OC-1%, and CRC-5.5%) [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref004" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3322/caac.21387" pmid="28055103" count="1">4</citation>].

Often the first malignancy affecting women with LS, EC provides a unique diagnostic opportunity [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref005" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/01.aog.0000154885.44002.ae" pmid="15738026" count="1">5</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Most women survive EC [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref006" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ijc.10667" pmid="12385019" count="1">6</citation>] but remain at increased risk of associated cancers, particularly CRC [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref007" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jnci/djs525" pmid="23385444" pmcid="PMC3576323" count="1">7</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Cascade testing of relatives generates on average 3 further diagnoses per index case [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref008" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa043146" pmid="15872200" count="1">8</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These <italic toggle="yes">path_MMR</italic> carriers can benefit from chemoprophylaxis [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref009" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0140-6736(11)61049-0" pmcid="PMC3243929" pmid="22036019" count="1">9</citation>], risk-reducing surgery [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref010" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa052627" pmid="16421367" count="1">10</citation>], family planning, and cancer surveillance [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref003" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/gutjnl-2015-309675" pmid="26657901" pmcid="PMC5534760" count="1">3</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Unselected screening of EC for MMR deficiency and/or microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H, a hallmark of MMR deficiency) has advantages that extend beyond LS carrier identification. <sentence_start/>Programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) blockade immunotherapy is most effective in MMR deficient tumours [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref011" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.aan6733" pmid="28596308" pmcid="PMC5576142" count="1">11</citation>], and molecular characterization defines prognosis and treatment eligibility [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref012" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/pas.0000000000000177" pmid="24503759" count="1">12</citation>].

<italic toggle="yes">Path_MMR</italic> carriers’ association with EC is well established [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref003" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/gutjnl-2015-309675" pmid="26657901" pmcid="PMC5534760" count="1">3</citation>]; however, the proportion of EC patients likely to test positive for LS is uncertain, with estimates spanning <1% to >10%. <sentence_start/>The variation in estimates comes from methodological heterogeneity, small sample sizes, and incomplete testing [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref013" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41436-019-0536-8" pmid="31086306" pmcid="PMC8076013" count="1">13</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Initial tumour triage by immunohistochemistry (IHC) and/or MSI with/without <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-methylation testing selects women for definitive constitutional analysis [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref014" ref-type="bibr" count="1">14</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, the diagnostic accuracy of these strategies is unknown in EC [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref015" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41436-019-0489-y" pmid="30918358" pmcid="PMC6774998" count="1">15</citation>]. <sentence_start/>For instance, MSI testing has reduced sensitivity in <italic toggle="yes">path</italic>_<italic toggle="yes">MSH6</italic> tumours [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref016" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1086/302612" pmid="10521294" pmcid="PMC1288281" count="1">16</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Selecting test populations by age and/or family history, failure to apply reference standard tests consistently, and poor conversion to definitive testing are all potential sources of bias [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref013" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41436-019-0536-8" pmid="31086306" pmcid="PMC8076013" count="1">13</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Most previous studies involve insurance-based healthcare systems; this is fraught with difficulty because fear of lack of reimbursement by services [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref017" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jlb/lsv008" pmid="26339500" pmcid="PMC4555880" count="1">17</citation>] and increased insurance premiums in individuals [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref018" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10897-006-9039-2" pmid="17106634" count="1">18</citation>] influences testing decisions. <sentence_start/>Thus, the aims of this prospective study were to (1) establish the prevalence of LS and (2) evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of common LS testing strategies in an unselected EC population within a non-insurance-based healthcare system.

The Proportion of Endometrial Tumours Associated with Lynch Syndrome (PETALS) study was sponsored by the University of Manchester, United Kingdom, and approved by the North West Research Ethics Committee (15/NW/0733; S1 Protocol). <sentence_start/>The study was prospectively registered (Cancer Research-UK clinical trial database, ref-13595). <sentence_start/>It is reported according to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guideline (S1 Checklist), and the primary data set is also provided (S1 Data).

Women were recruited from gynaecology clinics at Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust (MFT), a large gynaecological cancer centre, between October 2015 and January 2017. <sentence_start/>Women diagnosed with EC or atypical hyperplasia (AH) over the preceding 5 years were eligible for recruitment without demographic or histological restrictions. <sentence_start/>AH was included to capture the full spectrum of endometrial neoplasia. <sentence_start/>All women gave written, informed consent to participate, providing blood-DNA, tumour, and clinical data (age, body mass index [BMI], self-reported ethnicity) including detailed family histories (pedigrees). <sentence_start/>The latter were scored using revised Bethesda [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref019" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jnci/djh034" pmcid="PMC2933058" pmid="14970275" count="1">19</citation>], Amsterdam II [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref020" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0016-5085(99)70510-x" pmid="10348829" count="1">20</citation>], and Prediction of MMR Gene Mutations-v.5 scores (PREMM<sub>5</sub>) [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref021" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.2016.69.6120" pmcid="PMC5493047" pmid="28489507" count="1">21</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Additional samples were procured from women with EC who had consented to their clinical data, tumours, and DNA being used for future research between 2013 and 2014 at MFT; their detailed pedigrees were not available.

Hysterectomy and biopsy specimens were assessed by 2 specialist gynaecological pathologists according to FIGO-2009 staging criteria (EC) and WHO classification system (AH). <sentence_start/>Stromal tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) were reported as previously described [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref022" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/annonc/mdu450" pmid="25214542" pmcid="PMC6267863" count="1">22</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Tumour molecular profiling used the hysterectomy specimen when possible, but diagnostic endometrial specimens were used when hysterectomy was not performed or when equivocal IHC was repeated. <sentence_start/>All tissue was formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded according to local clinical protocols. <sentence_start/>Tissue blocks with the greatest tumour content (>70%) were chosen for DNA extraction. <sentence_start/>Tumour was either microdissected from 5 × 10 μm unstained sections or cored from tissue blocks, depending on tumour content. <sentence_start/>Nonmalignant adjacent tissue was selected for comparative constitutional MSI analysis.

IHC for the 4 MMR proteins was performed using the automated Ventana BenchMark ULTRA IHC⁄in situ hybridisation (ISH) staining module and the OptiView, 3′diaminobenzidine version 5 detection system (Ventana Co., USA) in a laboratory that participates successfully in external quality assurance (EQA; UK NEQAS ICC and ISH, Module 7B; ; S1 Text). <sentence_start/>The proportion of stained tumour epithelial component and intensity of staining was scored by 2 expert independent observers using tumour stroma as internal control as previously described [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref023" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/his.13925" pmid="31310679" count="1">23</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Examples of complete and ‘patchy’ MMR protein loss are illustrated in S1 Text.

MSI (and <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-methylation) analysis was performed in a UKAS ISO15189-accredited MSI testing reference laboratory that successfully participates in EQA ( ). <sentence_start/>DNA was extracted and underwent sodium bisulfite conversion using the Epitect Plus FFPE kit (Qiagen, UK). <sentence_start/>The MSI analysis system version 1.2 (Promega, USA) was used with standardised clinical protocols. <sentence_start/>Fluorescent-labelled primers were used to co-amplify 7 markers, including 5 mononucleotide-repeat markers (BAT-25, BAT-26, NR-21, NR-24, and MONO-27), and 2 control pentanucleotide-repeat markers (Penta-C/Penta-D). <sentence_start/>MSI status was determined by 2 independent scientists. <sentence_start/>Identical fragment profiles between tumour and matched normal tissue for all 5 mononucleotide loci was considered microsatellite stable (MSS); discordance in one mononucleotide locus was MSI low (MSI-L). <sentence_start/>Discordance in 2 or more mononucleotide loci was MSI high (MSI-H). <sentence_start/>Only those with MSI-H tumours were considered at risk of LS; this is consistent with expert consensus [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref015" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41436-019-0489-y" pmid="30918358" pmcid="PMC6774998" count="1">15</citation>].

Reflex <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-methylation testing was performed on MLH1 and/or PMS2-deficient and/or MSI tumours as previously described [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref024" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/jmedgenet-2014-102552" pmcid="PMC5159427" pmid="25280751" count="1">24</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Purified DNA was amplified with bisulfite specific primers in triplicate. <sentence_start/>An <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic> promoter region containing 4 CpG dinucleotides whose methylation status is strongly correlated with <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic> expression was analysed using pyrosequencing (PSQ 96MA). <sentence_start/>Two independent scientists interpreted the pyrograms. <sentence_start/>‘Hypermethylation’ described >10% mean methylation across the 4 CpG dinucleotides on over two-thirds of replicate analyses. <sentence_start/>A proportion of <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-hypermethylation cases underwent reference standard germline MMR sequencing to exclude co-existing <italic toggle="yes">path</italic>_<italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic> variants.

Indications for germline analysis were age <50 years; meeting revised Bethesda guidelines/Amsterdam II criteria; PREMM<sub>5</sub> score >10%; and indicative tumour molecular features, specifically MMR deficiency (MMRd, tumour epithelial loss of ≥1 MMR protein on IHC) and/or MSI-H unexplained by somatic <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-hypermethylation.

DNA was extracted from 2 mL lymphocyte blood (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid [EDTA] anticoagulant) using Chemagic DNA blood chemistry (CMG-1097-D) on an automated Perkin Elmer Chemagic-360 Magnetic Separation Module and a JANUS Integrator 4-tip Automated Liquid handling platform. <sentence_start/>DNA was eluted into 400 μL buffer. <sentence_start/>The concentration and quality of extracted DNA samples were measured using a Nanodrop ND-8000 spectrophotometer. <sentence_start/>MMR genes <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MSH2</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">MSH6</italic> were amplified using long-range polymerase chain reaction (PCR) followed by next generation sequencing (NGS) using Illumina SBS version 2 2 × 150 bp and Illumina MiSeq to analyse the coding region, flanking sequences to ±15 bp and known splicing variants (minimum 100× coverage depth) of <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">MSH2</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">MSH6</italic> (S1 Text). <sentence_start/>Variant identification and calling was via an in-house bioinformatic pipeline. <sentence_start/>Reported sequence changes and regions with <100× coverage were retested via Sanger sequencing using BigDye version 3.1. <sentence_start/>Copy number analysis to detect large genomic rearrangements affecting the MMR genes was performed using MLPA MRC-Holland probe mixes: P003-D1 <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">MSH2</italic> and P072-C1 <italic toggle="yes">MSH6</italic>. <sentence_start/>Variant nomenclature followed Human Genome Variation Society (HGVS) guidelines ( ) using reference sequences: LRG_216,t1(<italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>); LRG_218,t1(<italic toggle="yes">MSH2</italic>); LRG_219,t1(<italic toggle="yes">MSH6</italic>). <sentence_start/>Exons were numbered consecutively starting from exon 1 as the first translated exon for each probe mix. <sentence_start/>Cases with PMS2 protein loss, normal <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-methylation, and no <italic toggle="yes">path</italic>_<italic toggle="yes">MLH1/MSH2/MSH6</italic> variant underwent <italic toggle="yes">path</italic>_<italic toggle="yes">PMS2</italic> analysis at the regional specialist Yorkshire and North East Genomic Laboratory. <sentence_start/>When pathogenicity of the variant was unclear, Ian Frayling was consulted as InSiGHT representative to adjudicate. <sentence_start/>Somatic MMR sequencing was performed for discordant tumour/germline results (S1 Text).

We determined that a sample size of 497 was required to find a prevalence of LS-EC of 3% (95% confidence intervals 1.5%-4.5%) [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref025" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s12098-012-0763-3" pmid="22562262" count="1">25</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The statistical analysis plan was devised <italic toggle="yes">a priori</italic>. <sentence_start/>Diagnostic accuracy measures were conducted to establish the utility of clinical parameters and tumour triage strategies for risk stratifying women with EC for MMR germline sequencing, including age, family history, histological subtype, density of TILs, MMR deficiency by IHC, MSI status, and <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-methylation status. <sentence_start/>There were no data-driven changes to analyses. <sentence_start/>Descriptive univariate analysis was performed using Student <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> test or two-way ANOVA for normally distributed continuous variables, and Mann-Whitney U test for non-normally distributed continuous variables. <sentence_start/>Normality of the data was assessed by the Belanger and D’Agostino method with the Royston adjustment (alpha = 0.05) [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref026" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2307/2684359" count="1">26</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Pearson’s chi-squared test was used to test for independence of categorical variables. <sentence_start/>Diagnostic accuracy measures (sensitivity, specificity, and positive and negative predictive values) were calculated using standard formulae, with confidence intervals estimated by the Clopper-Pearson method. <sentence_start/>The reference standard was germline analysis and only women with <italic toggle="yes">path_MMR</italic> variants (not variants of unknown significance [VUS]) were considered to have LS (disease positive). <sentence_start/>Women were treated as disease negative (no LS) when germline analysis was not indicated. <sentence_start/>The exact McNemar’s test was used to compare the sensitivity and specificity of IHC-based versus MSI-based testing for LS identification. <sentence_start/>Logistic regression was used to identify clinical predictors of MSI, MMR deficiency, <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-hypermethylation, and germline <italic toggle="yes">path_MMR</italic> variants.

In total, 305 women were invited to participate in PETALS and undergo testing for LS (pedigree cohort). <sentence_start/>Only 2 declined, and 3 were ineligible (not EC/AH on final pathology; Fig 1). <sentence_start/>A further 200 women treated for AH/EC at MFT in the preceding 2 years (2013-2014) were included, but detailed family histories were unavailable (nonpedigree cohort). <sentence_start/>The final study population comprised 500 women with median age and BMI of 65-years and 32kg/m<sup>2</sup>, respectively, of predominantly white British ethnicity (81%; Table 1). <sentence_start/>There were 470 EC cases (94%) and 30 AH (6%). <sentence_start/>Most EC were low grade (62%) and early stage tumours (72%) of endometrioid subtype (70%). <sentence_start/>All 500 women underwent both MMR-IHC and MSI analysis, with targeted <italic toggle="yes">MLH1-</italic>methylation testing. <sentence_start/>Of these, 135 women underwent germline LS testing for the following indications: MSI-H MMR deficient tumour with normal <italic toggle="yes">MLH1-</italic>methylation (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 6); MSI-H MMR deficient tumour (<italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-methylation testing not indicated; <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 13); MMR deficient and MSS/MSI-L (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 19); MSI-H MMR-proficient tumour (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 6); age ≤50 years (n = 35); and strong family history (n = 12). <sentence_start/>A subset of women with tumour <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-hypermethylation (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 26) and subset of MSS/MSI-L patchy tumour MMR deficiency (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 18) also underwent testing (see Fig 1).

Methylation testing only done if ≥1 of MLH1 or PMS2 was lost on immunohistochemistry. <sentence_start/>“No methylation” denotes it was not indicated. <sentence_start/><sup>#</sup><italic toggle="yes">PMS2</italic> only tested if PMS2d and no <italic toggle="yes">path</italic>_<italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">path</italic>_<italic toggle="yes">MSH2</italic> or <italic toggle="yes">path</italic>_<italic toggle="yes">MSH6</italic>. <sentence_start/>^One of the MSI-H samples did not undergo germline testing as the patient died before blood could be taken. <sentence_start/>MSI, microsatellite instability; MSS, microsatellite stable; MMR, mismatch repair; MMRp, MMR proficient (no MMR protein loss); MMRd, MMR deficient (≥1 MMR protein lost).
Proportion of tumours associated with LS

We identified 16 <italic toggle="yes">path_MMR</italic> variant carriers, giving a 3.2% overall LS prevalence (95% CI 1.84%-5.14%). <sentence_start/>There were 8 <italic toggle="yes">path_MSH6</italic>, 4 <italic toggle="yes">path_MSH2</italic>, 2 <italic toggle="yes">path_MLH1</italic>, and 2 <italic toggle="yes">path_PMS2</italic> variant carriers (Table 2). <sentence_start/>Three had known LS, 2 died shortly after EC diagnosis, and the remaining 11 were offered, of whom 10 accepted, genetic counselling. <sentence_start/>To date, 14 relatives have also received genetic counselling. <sentence_start/>One woman carried 2 <italic toggle="yes">VUS</italic>_<italic toggle="yes">MSH6</italic>, considered pathogenic in combination (S2 Text). <sentence_start/>A further 10 women had MMR variants that were not recognized by InSiGHT ( ), including 5 previously unreported variants (S3 Text). <sentence_start/>Greatest discrepancy between IHC and MSI findings was observed for those with a germline path_<italic toggle="yes">MSH6</italic> variant with 5/8 demonstrating MSH6 loss on IHC but MSS. <sentence_start/>One path_<italic toggle="yes">MSH6</italic> variant (<italic toggle="yes">MSH6</italic> c.2731C>T p.(Arg911Ter) was observed in 3 index cases and therefore could represent a local founder mutation; however, review of the local clinical database indicates this variant only affects 5/487 of local LS families.
Selecting women for germline LS testing

In total, there were 73 women ≤50 years, of whom 7 (10%) had LS. <sentence_start/>All 7 had indicative tumour molecular features (MMRd ± MSI-H). <sentence_start/>Only screening women <50, <60, and <70 years would have missed 9, 6, and one LS diagnosis, respectively (Table 3). <sentence_start/>A further 35 women <50 years with MSS/MSI-L MMR-proficient tumours underwent germline testing for LS; 4 (11.4%) had <italic toggle="yes">VUS_MMR</italic>, but no further <italic toggle="yes">path_MMR</italic> variants were identified.

Comprehensive pedigree data were available for 300 women. <sentence_start/>Only 7/300 (2%) and 9/300 (3%) women with detailed pedigrees met the Amsterdam II criteria and revised Bethesda guidelines, of whom 4 (57%) and 5 (56%) had LS, respectively. <sentence_start/>All women with LS also had indicative tumour molecular features. <sentence_start/>The overall mean PREMM<sub>5</sub> score was 3.2% (SD 2.4%). <sentence_start/>A total of 164/299 (55%) women had scores greater than the 2.5% recommended cut-off for germline testing, with mean PREMM<sub>5</sub> score 4.3% in this subgroup, and 11 (6.7%) having LS. <sentence_start/>An additional 12 women with MSS/MSI-L MMR-proficient tumours underwent germline testing because of a previous LS-associated cancer (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3) or an indicative family history (including Amsterdam II [<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 2], revised Bethesda [<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 4], and PREMM<sub>5</sub> > 10% [<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3]). <sentence_start/>None carried a <italic toggle="yes">path_MMR</italic> variant or <italic toggle="yes">VUS_MMR</italic>.

In total 132/500 (26%) tumours were MMR deficient (Table 4), of which 83 were MSI-H. Women with MMR deficient tumours were older than those without MMR loss (mean difference 3.3 years, <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> test [unequal variances] <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.007). <sentence_start/>Of the 24 women who had tumours with patchy MMR loss, one had a germline <italic toggle="yes">VUS_MMR</italic> but none had LS. <sentence_start/>One MSS AH case had patchy MSH6 loss and was subsequently found to have a VUS_<italic toggle="yes">MSH6</italic>, but all other AH samples had intact MMR. <sentence_start/>Thirteen tumours failed first attempt but not repeat MMR-IHC testing.

In total, 89/500 (18%) tumours were MSI-H, and 21/500 (4%) were MSI-L. None of the 6 MSI-H MMR-proficient tumours were LS-associated (Table 4). <sentence_start/>Women with MSI-H tumours were older than those with MSS tumours (mean difference 4.7 years, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.001). <sentence_start/>Mononucleotides BAT-25 and/or BAT-26 accounted for 95% of MSI-H events. <sentence_start/>No AH samples were MSI-H. Eights tumours failed first attempt but not repeat MSI analysis.

In total, 100 tumours underwent reflex <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-methylation analysis because of MLH1-deficiency on IHC. <sentence_start/>Of these, 83 (16% of 500) were hypermethylated (Table 4), and none of the 26 hypermethylated cases (31%) who underwent germline analysis had LS. <sentence_start/>One sample failed <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-methylation analysis several times. <sentence_start/>Women with <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-hypermethylated tumours were older than those with MMR-proficient tumours (<italic toggle="yes">t</italic> test [unequal variance] <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.001) and those with normal <italic toggle="yes">MLH1-</italic>methylation MMR deficient tumours (<italic toggle="yes">t</italic> test [unequal variance] <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.0034). <sentence_start/>Of 15 women with normal <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-methylation MMR deficient tumours, 3 (20%) had LS, all of which had complete IHC loss (3/10, 30%).

Somatic MMR testing was performed when indicative tumour molecular features were unexplained by LS or <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-hypermethylation: MSI-H MMR deficient (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 8), MSS/MSI-L MMR deficient (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 7), MSI-H MMR-proficient (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 6), patchy MMR deficient (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 18), and germline <italic toggle="yes">VUS_MMR</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 1) cases (S4 Text). <sentence_start/>Six tumours failed (MSI-H MMR deficient [<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 2], MSI-H MMR-proficient [<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 1], and patchy MMR deficient [<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3] cases). <sentence_start/>This comprehensive testing left just 1.9% (2/106) MMR deficient tumours unexplained by a <italic toggle="yes">path_MMR</italic> variant/epigenetic silencing (Table 4).
Diagnostic test accuracy of tumour triage

MMR-IHC was superior to MSI analysis for the identification of LS (Table 3). <sentence_start/>Sensitivity and specificity were 100% versus 56.3% (16/16 versus 9/16; difference 43.75%, 95% CI 13.2%-74.3%, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.016) and 80.6% versus 83.5% (390/484 versus 404/484; difference −2.9%, 95% CI −5.2% to −0.6%, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.013), respectively. <sentence_start/>Specificity was increased to 97.7% for both MMR-IHC and MSI with reflex <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-methylation testing (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 1). <sentence_start/>The area under the ROC curve for PREMM<sub>5</sub> and age was 0.73 versus 0.71, respectively, with PREMM<sub>5</sub> superior to age, although neither matched MMR-IHC for selecting women for germline LS testing (S5 Text). <sentence_start/>Eleven LS-associated tumours (69%) were of pure endometrioid histotype, and 15 (94%) had high tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte counts. <sentence_start/>MMR germline sequencing was conducted for 135/500 women, which means that the sensitivity and specificity of tumour triage strategies for LS detection may be overestimated in this study, although the risk of LS in women with no clinical or tumour predictors is expected to be extremely low.

Increased age was positively associated with tumour MMR deficiency (OR 1.02, 95% CI 1.00-1.04, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.013), MSI-H (OR 1.03, 95% CI 1.01-1.05, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.003), and <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-hypermethylation (OR 1.04, 95% CI 1.02-1.06, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.001) (tumours in which methylation testing was not indicated were assumed to have normal <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic> methylation), whilst negatively associated with LS (0.95, 95% CI 0.92-0.99, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.006). <sentence_start/>PREMM<sub>5</sub> was positively associated with LS (OR 3.88, 95% CI 1.74-8.65, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.001) but not with tumour test outcomes (IHC, MSI, or <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-hypermethylation). <sentence_start/>BMI was negatively associated with MMR deficiency (OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.96-1.00, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.036) and marginally negatively associated with LS (OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.87-1.00, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.055). <sentence_start/>Smoking was not consistently associated with any test outcomes.

In this prospective study, we found a 3.2% prevalence of LS in an unselected EC population and established MMR-IHC with targeted <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-methylation testing as the most accurate method of selecting women for germline LS testing. <sentence_start/>MSI was insufficiently sensitive, missing nearly half of all LS-EC. <sentence_start/>Family history by PREMM<sub>5</sub> score showed excellent sensitivity but poor specificity; the reverse was true for Amsterdam II criteria/revised Bethesda guidelines. <sentence_start/>Restricting testing to women <60 years would miss a third of all LS cases, but only one case was >70 years.

The 3.2% prevalence of LS-EC is consistent with the results of our recent systematic review [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref013" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41436-019-0536-8" pmid="31086306" pmcid="PMC8076013" count="1">13</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Only 6 previous studies tested unselected EC populations of ≥500 women for LS, all of which were conducted in the insurance-based healthcare systems of the US and Australia [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref027" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ygyno.2014.06.009" pmid="24933100" pmcid="PMC4125501" count="1">27</citation>-<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref032" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/pas.0000000000000321" pmid="25229768" pmcid="PMC4361228" count="1">32</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This impacted both the proportion of eligible women consenting to study participation as well as their willingness to undergo definitive germline testing [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref017" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jlb/lsv008" pmid="26339500" pmcid="PMC4555880" count="1">17</citation>]. <sentence_start/>To our knowledge, this is the first unselected EC population-based study of LS testing conducted in the fully state-funded healthcare system of the UK. <sentence_start/>We recruited >99% of newly diagnosed EC patients attending our institution during the recruitment period, all tumours underwent both IHC and MSI analysis, and germline LS testing was conducted for 135/136 eligible women. <sentence_start/>We found MSI analysis had a poor sensitivity, most notably in <italic toggle="yes">path</italic>_<italic toggle="yes">MSH6</italic> carriers. <sentence_start/>This phenomenon has been described previously [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref016" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1086/302612" pmid="10521294" pmcid="PMC1288281" count="1">16</citation>]; however, no large EC studies to date have germline tested all women with both MMR deficient and MSI-H tumours to enable a direct comparison between the 2 tumour triage strategies [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref013" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41436-019-0536-8" pmid="31086306" pmcid="PMC8076013" count="1">13</citation>]. <sentence_start/>For example, Goodfellow and colleagues carried out germline LS testing on just 5% of their population-based cohort, including those with MSH6-deficient MSI-H tumours (15/107 MMR deficient tumours with normal <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic> methylation) but not MSH6-deficient MSI-L or MSS tumours (6/107); it is therefore not possible to calculate the sensitivity of MSI analysis for <italic toggle="yes">path</italic>_<italic toggle="yes">MSH6</italic> carriers from these data [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref029" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.2015.63.9518" pmid="26552419" pmcid="PMC4678181" count="1">29</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Hampel and colleagues found all 6 endometrial tumours from <italic toggle="yes">path</italic>_<italic toggle="yes">MSH6</italic> carriers were MMR deficient, but just 3/6 were MSI-H; despite this, tumours were triaged for MMR germline sequencing using the results of MSI analysis, and only a subset underwent MMR-IHC [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref008" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa043146" pmid="15872200" count="1">8</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Our comprehensive testing strategy also identified somatic <italic toggle="yes">path_MMR</italic> variants in MMR deficient and/or MSI-H tumours unexplained by LS. <sentence_start/>This had been noted to a lesser extent in previous studies [33,34] and is an important finding because it removes many of the tumours that would otherwise have been considered ‘Lynch-like’ and posed a clinical management dilemma [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref035" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41436-020-0820-7" pmid="32409734" count="1">35</citation>].

There were 5 key strengths to our study. <sentence_start/>First, we recruited 99% of eligible women, ensuring an unbiased population of consecutive patients unrestricted by age, histological subtype, or treatment modality. <sentence_start/>Recruitment rates of around 50% have been reported previously, mainly from insurance-based healthcare systems [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref028" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.2013.51.2129" pmid="24323032" pmcid="PMC4876359" count="1">28</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Second, all tumours underwent MMR-IHC, MSI, and targeted <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-methylation testing, and all but one woman with indicative tumour features underwent germline <italic toggle="yes">path_MMR</italic> testing. <sentence_start/>This compares favourably to most studies with incomplete testing [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref013" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41436-019-0536-8" pmid="31086306" pmcid="PMC8076013" count="1">13</citation>] and allowed us to test selection criteria and tumour-based triage strategies. <sentence_start/>Third, all analyses were carried out to quality-assured clinical standards in specialist pathology and genetics referral laboratories. <sentence_start/>Fourth, all but 2 of the 106 (1.9%) MMR deficient tumours were explained by <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-hypermethylation, somatic MMR mutation, or LS. <sentence_start/>Fifth, our inclusion of AH, part of the spectrum of LS-EC [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref036" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/cncr.28152" pmid="23760948" pmcid="PMC4120439" count="1">36</citation>], is unusual but justified because identifying LS in women with AH not only supports future risk-reducing interventions but also impacts their immediate treatment decisions.

The main limitation was failure to conduct germline LS sequencing on the whole study population. <sentence_start/>In total, 135/500 (27%) women underwent germline testing, including every woman with established clinical (age ≤50 years, positive family history) or tumour characteristics (MMR deficient or MSI-H unexplained by <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-hypermethylation) predictive of LS; thus the prevalence of LS in the 365 (73%) women who did not undergo germline LS sequencing is expected to be extremely low. <sentence_start/>Further, our 27% germline sequencing rate is considerably higher than that reported by other population-based studies in EC [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref013" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41436-019-0536-8" pmid="31086306" pmcid="PMC8076013" count="1">13</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Other limitations include the small sample size with concomitantly few LS diagnoses and correspondingly wide CIs around our sensitivity and specificity estimates. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, our study was large enough to detect a significant difference in sensitivity between MMR deficiency and MSI-based tumour triage. <sentence_start/>All women were treated at one gynaecological cancer centre in North West England; although this might hinder generalizability to other populations, the clinicopathological characteristics of our EC population reflect the UK national picture. <sentence_start/>The relatively high proportion of <italic toggle="yes">path_MSH6</italic> variant carriers in our cohort affected the sensitivity of MSI-based tumour triage, and our study may underestimate its true value within a wider geographical distribution, although 2 women with <italic toggle="yes">path</italic>_<italic toggle="yes">MSH2</italic> and homozygous <italic toggle="yes">path</italic>_<italic toggle="yes">PMS2</italic> variants also demonstrated MSS tumour phenotypes. <sentence_start/>Pedigree data were not available for all patients and were self-reported and therefore prone to error, mirroring the situation in routine clinical practice.

Our findings support the unselected screening of EC for LS. <sentence_start/>We show that age, family history, and pathological findings are of limited value in selecting women for testing. <sentence_start/>Universal germline testing is not financially feasible [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref037" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fonc.2019.00061" pmid="30863719" pmcid="PMC6399107" count="1">37</citation>], mandating tumour-based triage. <sentence_start/>How best to achieve this is contentious, but the prevailing wisdom is that MSI and IHC are equivalent [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref029" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.2015.63.9518" pmid="26552419" pmcid="PMC4678181" count="1">29</citation>], despite limited evidence to support this [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref015" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41436-019-0489-y" pmid="30918358" pmcid="PMC6774998" count="1">15</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Our data provide strong evidence that MMR-IHC with targeted <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-methylation testing is superior to MSI-based testing in EC. <sentence_start/>It reduces the proportion of women requiring germline sequencing without missing any cases, lowering costs [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref037" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fonc.2019.00061" pmid="30863719" pmcid="PMC6399107" count="1">37</citation>], and improving cost-effectiveness [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref038" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0221419" pmid="31469860" pmcid="PMC6716649" count="1">38</citation>, <citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref039" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/jcm9061664" pmid="32492863" pmcid="PMC7356917" count="1">39</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The identification of MMR deficient EC is of clinical importance. <sentence_start/>It allows clinicians to tailor treatments [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref040" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/modpathol.2015.43" pmid="25720322" count="1">40</citation>], explain prognosis [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref040" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/modpathol.2015.43" pmid="25720322" count="1">40</citation>], predict cancer recurrence [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref041" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ygyno.2017.07.003" pmid="28709704" pmcid="PMC5601318" count="1">41</citation>], and individualize follow-up [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref041" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ygyno.2017.07.003" pmid="28709704" pmcid="PMC5601318" count="1">41</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, women want to be tested; it is striking that 99% of eligible women approached during routine gynaecological cancer care agreed to participate, and 10/11 newly identified LS carriers attended genetic counselling and supported cascade testing of at-risk family members.

Unselected screening of EC for LS leads to the discovery of VUS_MMR. <sentence_start/>These create a clinical conundrum because new variants can be challenging to classify. <sentence_start/>Indeed, 15 of our 27 MMR variants were not previously reported to either the ClinVar or InSiGHT data sets. <sentence_start/>This highlights the need for international multidisciplinary expert teams to explore the clinical significance of VUS_MMR and/or investment in saturation genome editing platforms for high throughput analysis [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref015" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41436-019-0489-y" pmid="30918358" pmcid="PMC6774998" count="1">15</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Such infrastructure is established for MMR variant interpretation and behoves all clinical laboratories to interpret variants according to a single set of defined criteria ( ) before universal screening for LS in EC begins in earnest.

To our knowledge, this is the most comprehensive study to date exploring the prevalence of LS in an unselected EC population treated within a non-insurance-based healthcare system. <sentence_start/>Consent for LS testing was taken by gynaecologists during routine clinical care [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref042" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/jcm9061842" pmid="32545685" pmcid="PMC7355853" count="1">42</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In this cohort, we found IHC outperforms MSI as a means of tumour-based triage and reliably identifies both germline and somatic MMR deficient tumours to inform clinical care. <sentence_start/>The overall prevalence of LS in EC was 3.2%, which is comparable to that of CRC [<citation rid="pmed.1003263.ref030" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15872200" doi="10.1056/NEJMoa043146" count="1">30</citation>], and justifies a similar recommendation for unselected LS screening. <sentence_start/>We endorse, when resources allow, the universal screening of EC for LS using IHC, targeted <italic toggle="yes">MLH1</italic>-methylation testing, and, where indicated, germline sequencing for <italic toggle="yes">path_MMR</italic> variants.
